title: RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution

paper.title: RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent focus in agentic reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to improve credit assignment in long-horizon tasks. One promising direction combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), integrating trajectory-level advantages with dense token-level supervision. This line of work often conditions a teacher model on privileged context, such as agentic skills, to score tokens generated by the student policy. Despite their progress, they largely overlook ❶ the on-policy evolution of agentic skills and ❷ the reliability of teacher supervision. Towards this end, we introduce Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that enables agentic skills and the policy model to co-evolve throughout the training process. Specifically, RSIPO enables the policy itself to extract skills from completed trajectories and explicitly optimizes its skill-generation capability through trajectory replay. It further employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to dynamically calibrate the student’s trust in teacher scores, accounting for the fact that skill-enhanced teacher guidance can sometimes be less reliable. Experiments with Qwen-family models on embodied interaction and search-based agentic tasks demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms all the compared baseline approaches. With Qwen2.5-7B as the base model, RSIPO achieves an average success rate of 98.6% on ALFWorld, yielding absolute improvements of 2.5% and 17.4% over the second-best baseline and standard GRPO, respectively.
Code is available at https://github.com/zfkarl/RSIPO .

Code is available at https://github.com/zfkarl/RSIPO . 1 Introduction Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) has emerged as a key component of large language model (LLM) post-training, substantially improving model performance on long-horizon multi-turn tasks. Unlike conventional RL for static and single-turn scenarios Guo et al. (2025) , agentic RL aims to train models through interactions with dynamic environments, where they iteratively reason, invoke tools, and incorporate observations across multi-turn conversations Lu et al. (2026b) ; Singh et al. (2025) . This requires learning sequential decision-making policies that reliably guide agents toward successful task completion. Figure 1: Comparison of three paradigms of agentic RL. (a) RLVR-based methods assign equal trajectory-level advantages to all response tokens. (b) OPSD-based methods provide token-level supervision from a self-teacher. (c) Hybrid methods combine the two branches, typically using agentic skills as the teacher’s privileged context. As shown in Figure 1 , recent agentic RL approaches have explored reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), and hybrid training frameworks that combine the two. Among them, RLVR-based methods provide effective outcome-based trajectory-level advantages, whereas OPSD-based methods offer dense and fine-grained token-level supervision. Hybrid methods seek to combine these complementary signals, typically coupling an RLVR branch with an OPSD branch for joint optimization. In the OPSD branch, a teacher model conditioned on privileged context scores student-generated tokens, and the student is trained to reduce the token-level log-probability gap between the two models. For example, SDAR Lu et al. (2026a) uses agentic skills retrieved from an external skill library as privileged context for the teacher model, whereas OPID Yang et al. (2026b) and SEED Wu et al. (2026) explore generating such skills with external or internal analyzers. Despite their progress in advancing agentic RL, existing hybrid approaches face two key limitations. First, agentic skills are either retrieved from a static external library or produced by a skill generator trained off-policy in advance. Consequently, while the policy improves at task execution during training, skill generation is not explicitly optimized on-policy to evolve alongside it. Following the experimental setup of SEED Wu et al. (2026) , we find that only 0.25% of the trajectories in the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data used to train the skill generator are successful, mainly because the base model follows the required action format in just 11.0% of its steps, whereas the policy’s rollout success rate rapidly exceeds 80% during subsequent RL training (Figure 2 (a)). As a result, 86.8% of the skills in the SFT data concern action format or syntax, even though 99.7% of the policy’s actions are already valid in the first 10 RL steps. The trajectories that the skill generator must summarize thus shift from almost exclusively failures to predominantly successes, creating a distribution shift that its initial off-policy training does not explicitly address. Second, the OPSD objective encourages the student to align with a skill-enhanced teacher, implicitly assuming that the teacher consistently provides more reliable guidance than the student’s own decisions. However, access to skills does not guarantee better performance. As shown in Figure 2 (b), the skill-enhanced teacher underperforms the student on 5.5%–22.4% of tasks across different levels of student competence. Its advantage is most pronounced on tasks that the student solves in one to three of four rollouts. By contrast, for tasks with zero or four successful student rollouts, the proportions of tasks on which the teacher outperforms and underperforms the student differ only slightly (16.0% vs. 13.6% and 6.9% vs. 5.5%, respectively). Figure 2 (c) further shows that, during the first 15 RL training steps, the teacher underperforms the student on more tasks than it outperforms the student (22.9% vs. 15.0%) and continues to underperform on 4%–11% of tasks thereafter. Therefore, uniformly trusting teacher guidance exposes the student policy to unreliable supervision. Figure 2: Preliminary analysis with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ALFWorld. (a) Success rate of the skill generator rollouts on SFT data and of the policy rollouts during RL training. (b) Share of training tasks on which the skill-enhanced teacher succeeds more or less often than the student, grouped by the student’s successes in four separate rollouts on the task. (c) The same shares over RL training, averaged over blocks of 15 steps. These observations motivate Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that jointly improves skill generation and task execution while calibrating the student’s trust in teacher supervision. Building on the RLVR and OPSD branches, RSIPO uses the student policy to rewrite skills and replays half of its rollouts with these skills, measuring the resulting gains relative to the remaining half, which serves as a control group. Each replay gain is centered by subtracting the mean gain for the same task type, and the resulting reward is assigned to the generated skill tokens. This explicitly optimizes the policy’s skill-generation capability on-policy without requiring auxiliary judge models or additional evaluation data. Beyond skill evolution, RSIPO dynamically adjusts the student’s reliance on the teacher in the OPSD branch. Specifically, it applies empirical Bayes shrinkage to the replay gains to obtain robust and task-dependent trust coefficients that weight the OPSD objective. These coefficients increase the student’s reliance on reliable teacher guidance, downweight unreliable supervision, and can disable distillation entirely on tasks where the teacher is particularly unreliable. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple base models on ALFWorld Shridhar et al. (2021) for embodied interaction and seven datasets for search-based agentic tasks. The results show that RSIPO substantially outperforms a wide range of baselines, including RLVR-based, OPSD-based, and hybrid agentic RL methods. On ALFWorld, RSIPO achieves average task success rates of 95.7% and 98.6% with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B Yang et al. (2024) , respectively, surpassing the strongest prior method, SEED Wu et al. (2026) , by 3.9% and 2.5%. The performance improvements over the standard GRPO+OPSD baseline are even larger, reaching 14.5% and 18.2%, respectively. To summarize, our main contributions of this paper are threefold: ❶ Co-Evolving Perspective. We identify limitations in skill generation and teacher supervision in existing agentic RL methods and propose a co-evolving perspective that couples on-policy skill improvement with adaptive trust in the teacher. ❷ Self-Evolving Framework. We introduce RSIPO, a self-evolving framework that uses skill-induced performance gains measured through trajectory replay to drive skill-policy co-evolution and applies empirical Bayes shrinkage to calibrate the student’s trust in teacher supervision. ❸ Empirical Validation. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms existing agentic RL methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ALFWorld and search-based agentic tasks. 2 Related Work 2.1 Agentic Reinforcement Learning Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated substantial gains in single-turn reasoning. Critic-free methods such as GRPO Guo et al. (2025) and DAPO Yu et al. (2025) estimate advantages from group-normalized outcome rewards, eliminating the need for the learned value network used in PPO Schulman et al. (2017) . In agentic settings, policies interact with embodied Shridhar et al. (2021) , shopping Yao et al. (2022) , or search Jin et al. (2025) environments over multiple turns. Attributing a single terminal reward to a long sequence of decisions poses a credit assignment challenge, motivating multi-turn training frameworks Wang et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) and step-level advantage estimation Feng et al. (2025) . A complementary line of work equips agents with reusable natural-language experience, including reflections, insights, and skill libraries Shinn et al. (2023) ; Zhao et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2023) , with recent methods incorporating such skills into agentic RL training Xia et al. (2026) ; Lu et al. (2026b) . These approaches, however, typically rely on fixed skill libraries, frozen external generators, or skill-generation objectives that do not explicitly account for the utility of generated skills in task execution. 2.2 On-Policy Self-Distillation Figure 3: Overview of the proposed RSIPO framework. Replay gains measured by the execution check reward on-policy skill generation and calibrate the student’s trust in the skill-enhanced teacher. In on-policy distillation (OPD), a teacher model scores sequences sampled from the student policy, allowing the student to learn from its own generation distribution rather than a fixed corpus Agarwal et al. (2024) ; Gu et al. (2024) . On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as the teacher by conditioning it on privileged training-time context unavailable to the student, such as worked solutions or feedback on the student’s attempts Zhao et al.
